title: How Coordinators Can Set Up Realistic Fall Calendars
summary: A practical guide for IB DP coordinators to map official deadlines, spread fall assessments, protect feedback time, and manage student exceptions.
body_markdown:
A realistic fall assessment calendar does more than distribute deadlines evenly. It works backward from official IB requirements, limits simultaneous student demands, accounts for teacher marking capacity, and preserves time for feedback, authentication, standardization, and unexpected disruption.


For many schools, September-November combines DP2 coursework, predicted-grade evidence, university applications, core requirements, and normal teaching. Coordinators must therefore review these demands together rather than allowing departments to schedule them independently.


### Start with official requirements


Check the current session's **Diploma Programme Assessment procedures** , subject guides, IBIS notices, and Programme Resource Centre materials. The IB establishes examination schedules and submission procedures, while schools administer registration and assessment according to the[current DP general regulations](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/become-an-ib-school/pdfs/dp-2026-general-regulations.pdf) .


Many dates described as “IB deadlines” are actually **internal school deadlines** . These should come early enough to allow authentication, marking, standardization, administrative checks, student absence, and technical problems. Never copy another school's dates without verifying the examination session, subject requirements, and local calendar.


The master calendar should include:


- Official registration and submission requirements
- Internal and externally assessed coursework
- TOK essay, exhibition, EE, and CAS milestones
- Predicted-grade evidence and reporting dates
- University application deadlines
- Holidays, trips, performances, and oral examinations
- Marking, standardization, and upload periods


The[IB overview of DP assessment](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/) confirms that the programme combines external and internal assessment. A complete calendar must therefore account for tests, oral work, investigations, performances, coursework, and the DP core.


### Build one cohort-wide assessment map


Ask every subject teacher and core supervisor to enter planned assessments into one shared calendar. Record the cohort, purpose, estimated student workload, marking time, feedback date, draft status, and whether the date can move.


Assessment type Examples Scheduling implication


Fixed external requirement Examination or IB submission process Verify first and protect an administrative buffer


School-controlled assessment Timed essay, test, practical Moveable, but must provide valid evidence


Coursework milestone Proposal, draft, final hand-in Schedule as a sequence, not one deadline


Core milestone EE meeting, TOK stage, CAS review Coordinate because many candidates are affected


Formative checkpoint Outline, practice response, quiz Keep low stakes and connect it to later work


Colour-coding helps reveal collisions, but a short quiz and a final IA submission are not equivalent. Add a workload rating such as **light, moderate, or heavy** , then inspect the combinations faced by actual students.


### Apply a weekly capacity rule


A practical starting recommendation is no more than **two heavy assessment events per student per week** , including no more than one final coursework submission. This is not an IB rule, and schools may adjust it for their timetable and context.


Count preparation time as well as due dates. Two Friday submissions still collide if both require sustained work during the same preceding week. A simple scoring system can support discussion:


- Light formative task: 1 point
- Moderate test or substantial draft: 2 points
- Major test, oral, or final submission: 3 points


The exact threshold matters less than using one transparent method across departments. When a week becomes overloaded, move the most flexible school-controlled task rather than an official requirement.


### Plan September-November in phases


### September: verify and diagnose


Confirm registrations, subjects, levels, candidate details, access arrangements, and current component requirements. Audit the status of each IA, EE, TOK requirement, and CAS process instead of relying only on verbal assurances.


Early assessments should diagnose performance and generate useful feedback. Avoid clustering final submissions immediately after a long break, particularly for students who have changed schools or programmes.


### October: gather balanced evidence


October often carries university application pressure and predicted-grade decisions. Publish what evidence teachers may consider, when departmental standardization occurs, and when predictions become final under school policy. A predicted grade should reflect a relevant body of evidence rather than one conveniently timed test.


Spread major assessments across different weeks and reserve marking time after each. Departments may use[RevisionDojo's Questionbank and timed assessment tools](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-for-ib-teachers-departments) for diagnosis, but teachers must interpret platform-generated results professionally.


### November: consolidate progress


Use November to complete agreed milestones, address missing work, and act on feedback. Do not fill every available week simply because December remains open. Teachers need time to standardize marks, and coordinators need capacity for exceptions.


For May-session schools, November is usually a staging period rather than the final IB submission month. For November-session schools, examinations and session administration dominate, so planning must follow the current[IB examination schedule](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/exam-schedule/) and protect examination security.


### Schedule the work behind each deadline


A final hand-in is only the end of a longer process. Backward planning should include:


1. Task briefing and criteria clarification
2. Research, experimentation, or preparation
3. Progress checkpoint
4. Permitted teacher feedback
5. Student revision and final submission
6. Authentication and academic integrity review
7. Marking, standardization, verification, and upload buffer


The IB's[academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) emphasizes that teachers should see work develop and be satisfied that it is the student's own. Compressing substantial coursework into one short period weakens supervision and makes authentication harder.


The[RevisionDojo Coursework Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader) can provide formative, criterion-related observations on drafts. Teachers must still follow current subject guides, permitted-feedback rules, school policy, and professional judgment.


### Protect marking and feedback capacity


Every student deadline creates another staff deadline. If several subjects assess simultaneously, the following week may become unmanageable for marking, moderation, reteaching, and individual support.


Record an expected feedback date beside each significant assessment. If that date is unrealistic, the assessment date probably is too. The[IB assessment guide for teachers and coordinators](https://www.ibo.org/contentassets/4d92e48d38a4415a87e11555e143a39f/assessment-guide-for-teachers-and-coordinators-en.pdf) identifies formative feedback as an important teacher responsibility throughout the course.


A timed section, oral conference, or selected questions may sometimes provide enough evidence without another full paper. Reserve complete mocks for points when students have covered sufficient material and can act on the results. The[RevisionDojo mock-exam guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-mock-exams) explains how to use timed practice diagnostically.


### Control changes and exceptions


Publish who may move deadlines, how much notice is expected, and how changes will be communicated. Establish procedures for illness, access arrangements, transfers, technology failure, academic integrity concerns, and conflicts with major school obligations.


Avoid relying on informal private extensions. Record exceptions confidentially and review the student's position across all subjects so that solving one clash does not create another.


### Test and publish the calendar


Review the plan from three perspectives: a student taking a demanding subject combination, the staff who must mark work the following week, and the coordinator responsible for externally consequential dates. Verify official requirements using current IB systems and documents.


Publish one authoritative version and label dates as **draft** , **final** , **internal** , or **official IB** . RevisionDojo's[IB subject resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib) and[IB Grade Calculator](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/grade-calculator) can support preparation and indicative analysis, but estimates must not be presented as official grades.


### Conclusion


Realistic fall calendars begin with verified requirements, map demands across the whole cohort, limit weekly load, and protect feedback and administration time. September should verify and diagnose, October should gather balanced evidence, and November should consolidate progress. RevisionDojo Questionbank practice, coursework feedback, and mock assessments can then support learning between major deadlines without adding unnecessary compulsory work.
